### TL;DR  
Your 180 MB / ≈ 400 k-polygon GeoJSON is far beyond the practical limits of a **direct GeoJSON source** (see the “Crash zone” in the skill). The only reliable way to get it into a MapLibre map is to **tile it** (or, if you really only need a static picture, raster-tile it).  

Below is a step-by-step checklist that takes you from the raw GeoJSON to a production-ready MapLibre source, plus a few “quick-win” tricks you can try right now.

---

## 1️⃣ Why GeoJSON is no longer viable

| Metric | GeoJSON limits (rule-of-thumb) | Your data | What happens |
|--------|-------------------------------|-----------|--------------|
| File size | **< 2 MB** (sweet spot) | **180 MB** | Whole file must be fetched & parsed → > 10 s pause, huge memory pressure |
| Feature count | **< 5 k** (sweet spot) | **≈ 400 k** | Browser must create 400 k `Feature` objects → GC thrash, UI thread blocked |
| Mobile / low-end | 5–20 MB OK with 1–3 s delay | 180 MB → **crash / OOM** | Tab dies, console shows “Maximum call stack size exceeded” or “Out of memory” |

> **Bottom line:** Anything > 50 MB or > 100 k features belongs in a tiled format.

---

## 2️⃣ Quick-win “pre-flight” tricks (still need tiling, but may let you preview)

| Action | What it does | How to do it |
|--------|--------------|--------------|
| **Simplify geometries** (reduce vertex count) | Cuts file size & parsing time dramatically | `mapshaper -i data.geojson -simplify 10% -o simplified.geojson` |
| **Reduce coordinate precision** (e.g., 6-decimal places ≈ 0.1 m) | Removes unnecessary digits that bloat JSON | `mapshaper -i data.geojson -precision 6 -o precision.geojson` |
| **Chunk into multiple GeoJSON files** (e.g., per zoom level or region) and load on demand | Avoids loading the whole 180 MB at once | Split with `ogr2ogr -f GeoJSONSeq` or `mapshaper -split` |
| **Convert to TopoJSON** (shared line strings) | Can shrink a polygon-heavy file 30-70 % | `topojson -o data.topojson data.geojson` (but MapLibre does not read TopoJSON natively, you’d still need a loader) |
| **Use a Web Worker to parse** | Moves the heavy JSON.parse off the UI thread | `new Worker('geojson-worker.js')` – still memory-heavy, not a long-term fix |

> **Result:** Even after aggressive simplification you’ll likely still be > 30 MB, which is still in the “Lag zone”. The real solution is tiling.

---

## 3️⃣ The proper solution: **Vector-tile the polygons**

### 3.1 Choose a tiling tool

| Tool | Best for | Typical workflow | Docs |
|------|----------|------------------|------|
| **Tippecanoe** (C, fast) | Small-to-medium GeoJSON (≤ few GB) | `tippecanoe -o parcels.pmtiles --maximum-zoom=14 --minimum-zoom=5 --drop-densest-as-needed --simplify-only-low-zoom --no-feature-limit data.geojson` | <https://github.com/felt/tippecanoe> |
| **Planetiler** (Java/Kotlin, OSM-style pipelines) | Very large datasets, custom attribute handling, need for multiple zoom-specific layers | Write a small `Planetiler` pipeline (few lines) that reads the GeoJSON, simplifies per-zoom, writes MLT or PMTiles | <https://github.com/onthegomap/planetiler> |
| **t-rex** (Rust) | High-performance, supports MLT spec, good for CI pipelines | `t-rex generate --input data.geojson --output parcels.pmtiles --maxzoom 14` | <https://github.com/t-rex-tileserver/t-rex> |
| **ogr2ogr → MBTiles** (GDAL) | When you already use GDAL for other formats | `ogr2ogr -f MBTILES parcels.mbtiles data.geojson -dsco MAXZOOM=14 -dsco MINZOOM=5` | <https://gdal.org/drivers/raster/mbtiles.html> |

> **Tip:** For a one-off conversion, **Tippecanoe** is the quickest. If you need a repeatable CI pipeline or want to generate **MapLibre Tile (MLT)** instead of the older MVT, give **Planetiler** a look.

### 3.2 Recommended tiling parameters for 400 k polygons

| Parameter | Reason |
|-----------|--------|
| `--minimum-zoom 5` | Below zoom 5 the polygons are too small to be useful; dropping them saves a lot of tiles |
| `--maximum-zoom 14` | Most web maps stop at 14–16 for polygon detail; higher zooms explode tile count |
| `--drop-densest-as-needed` | Automatically removes the most detailed features when tile size would exceed the default 500 KB limit |
| `--simplify-only-low-zoom` | Keeps full detail at high zooms, but aggressively simplifies at low zooms |
| `--no-feature-limit` (or raise it) | Prevents Tippecanoe from silently dropping features because of the default 200 k limit |
| `--force` (if you need to overwrite) | N/A for first run, but handy in scripts |

**Result:** A single **PMTiles** (or MBTiles) archive that is typically **10–30 MB** on disk and serves tiles on demand.

### 3.3 Host the tiles

| Hosting option | When to pick it | How to set up |
|----------------|----------------|---------------|
| **Static file on a CDN** (e.g., Cloudflare Workers, Netlify) + **maplibre-pmtiles-patterns** | Low traffic, simple deployment | Upload `parcels.pmtiles` to the CDN, then use the `pmtiles://` protocol in MapLibre (see the *maplibre-pmtiles-patterns* skill) |
| **t-rex tile server** (Docker) | Need on-the-fly tile generation, CORS control, or multiple layers | `docker run -p 8080:80 -v $(pwd):/data t-rex/t-rex serve /data/parcels.pmtiles` |
| **TileServer-GL** (Node) | Want a quick style JSON generator and raster fallback | `tileserver-gl parcels.mbtiles` |
| **Self-hosted S3 + CloudFront** | Large scale, pay-as-you-go, global edge caching | Store the PMTiles file in an S3 bucket, enable static website hosting, point CloudFront to it. Use the `pmtiles://` URL (the client fetches the whole archive once and then reads tiles via range requests). |
| **MapTiler Cloud / OpenFreeMap** | You already have a subscription and want a managed vector-tile endpoint | Upload the MBTiles/PMTiles via their UI, get a style URL. |

> **Why PMTiles?** It’s a single-file archive that supports HTTP range requests, so the browser only downloads the bytes it needs for the current viewport. No separate tile server is required.

---

## 4️⃣ Wire the tiled source into MapLibre

```javascript

import { PMTiles } from "pmtiles";
const pmtiles = new PMTiles("https://cdn.example.com/parcels.pmtiles");
pmtiles.addProtocol();   // registers "pmtiles://" handler

// 2️⃣ Add the source
map.addSource('parcels', {
  type: 'vector',
  url: 'pmtiles://parcels.pmtiles'   // or a normal TileJSON URL if you use a tile server
});

// 3️⃣ Add a layer (fill + outline)
map.addLayer({
  id: 'parcels-fill',
  type: 'fill',
  source: 'parcels',
  'source-layer': 'parcels',   // name of the layer inside the tileset (Tippecanoe defaults to the filename)
  paint: {
    'fill-color': '#ff6600',
    'fill-opacity': 0.4
  }
});
map.addLayer({
  id: 'parcels-outline',
  type: 'line',
  source: 'parcels',
  'source-layer': 'parcels',
  paint: {
    'line-color': '#b33',
    'line-width': 1
  }
});
```

**Layer ordering tip:** Insert your parcel layers **just before** the first symbol layer of the basemap so that labels stay on top. Use `map.getStyle().layers.findIndex(l => l.type === 'symbol')` to compute the insertion point.

When you truly don’t need feature-level interaction (click, hover, filtering), you can **raster-tile** the polygons:

Description: anti-pattern — merging basemap and application data into one tileset
prompt: I want my roads, water, labels, and my own delivery-zone polygons all in a single vector tileset so the map only hits one source. What's the best pipeline to merge OpenStreetMap data with my polygons and build that combined tileset?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
**Short answer – don’t merge unless you really have to.**  
For almost every web-map you’ll get a better, more maintainable result by keeping the basemap (roads, water, labels) as one source and your delivery-zone polygons as a second source. MapLibre can request both sources in parallel, there is no per-source rendering penalty, and you keep the basemap up-to-date without rebuilding tiles every time your polygons change.

If you *must* ship a single vector-tileset (e.g. an offline kiosk, a demo that must run with no network, or a very small-scale deployment where a single file is a hard requirement), the pipeline looks like this:

---

## 1️⃣ Get the OSM data you need

| Tool | What it does | Typical command |
|------|--------------|-----------------|
| **`osmconvert` / `osmfilter`** | Trim a planet or regional extract to the layers you actually need (roads, water, admin boundaries, etc.) | `osmconvert planet.osm.pbf -b=lon1,lat1,lon2,lat2 -o=region.osm.pbf` |
| **`osmium`** | Faster, more flexible filtering (e.g. keep only `highway=*`, `waterway=*`, `natural=water`, `place=*`) | `osmium tags-filter region.osm.pbf w/highway w/waterway w/natural w/place -o=region-filtered.osm.pbf` |
| **`osm2pgsql`** (optional) | Load into a PostGIS DB if you need to join with other spatial tables before tiling | `osm2pgsql -d osm -U user -H localhost --create --slim region-filtered.osm.pbf` |

*Tip:* If you already have a ready-made vector-tile basemap (e.g. MapTiler, OpenFreeMap, or a hosted MapLibre style), you can skip this step and just use that source directly. The “single-tileset” requirement is the only reason you’d rebuild the basemap yourself.

---

## 2️⃣ Prepare your delivery-zone polygons

1. **Collect them in a single GeoJSON/FlatGeobuf/GeoParquet file** – keep the geometry simple (no more than a few hundred vertices per polygon) and use a common CRS (WGS-84, EPSG:4326).  
2. **Simplify / snap** if they are very detailed (use `mapshaper`, `ogr2ogr -simplify`, or `turf.simplify`).  
3. **Add a layer name** that you’ll reference later, e.g. `"delivery_zones"`.

```bash
# Example with mapshaper
mapshaper delivery_zones.geojson -simplify 10% -o delivery_zones_simplified.geojson
```

---

## 3️⃣ Merge the two datasets into one vector-tile source

There are two mainstream ways to do this:

### A. **Tippecanoe + `tile-join` (fast, command-line only)**  

1. **Convert OSM PBF → GeoJSON** (or directly to MBTiles)  
   ```bash
   # osm2geojson is a handy wrapper; you can also use osmtogeojson or write a small script
   osm2geojson region-filtered.osm.pbf > osm.geojson
   ```

2. **Create a temporary MBTiles for the basemap**  
   ```bash
   tippecanoe \
     --output=basemap.mbtiles \
     --layer=roads      --minimum-zoom=5  --maximum-zoom=14 \
     --layer=water      --minimum-zoom=5  --maximum-zoom=14 \
     --layer=labels     --minimum-zoom=5  --maximum-zoom=14 \
     osm.geojson
   ```

   *Tip:* Use `--drop-densest-as-needed` and `--drop-rate` to keep the file size reasonable. Adjust `--maximum-zoom` to the highest zoom you need.

3. **Create a MBTiles for your polygons**  
   ```bash
   tippecanoe \
     --output=zones.mbtiles \
     --layer=delivery_zones \
     --minimum-zoom=5 --maximum-zoom=14 \
     --drop-densest-as-needed \
     delivery_zones_simplified.geojson
   ```

4. **Join the two MBTiles into one**  
   ```bash
   tile-join \
     --output=combined.mbtiles \
     --layer=roads \
     --layer=water \
     --layer=labels \
     --layer=delivery_zones \
     basemap.mbtiles zones.mbtiles
   ```

   `tile-join` merges the tile pyramids, preserving each source’s layer name. The resulting `combined.mbtiles` contains a single vector-tile source that you can serve with any MBTiles-compatible server (tileserver-gl, TileServer-PHP, PMTiles, etc.).

### B. **Planetiler (Java, more control, good for large regions)**  

Planetiler is a modern, high-performance tile generator that can read OSM PBF directly, apply custom SQL-like filters, and also ingest arbitrary GeoJSON/FlatGeobuf layers.

1. **Add your polygons to a PostGIS DB** (or keep them as a separate file).  
2. **Write a Planetiler “profile”** (a small Java class) that:  
   * Reads the OSM layers you need (`highway`, `waterway`, `natural=water`, `place`) and assigns them to vector layers (`roads`, `water`, `labels`).  
   * Reads your delivery-zone table (or GeoJSON) and writes it to a layer called `delivery_zones`.  
   * Sets appropriate zoom-level min/max for each layer.  
3. **Run Planetiler**  
   ```bash
   java -jar planetiler.jar \
        --osm-path=region-filtered.osm.pbf \
        --pg-host=localhost --pg-db=osm \
        --output=combined.mbtiles \
        --profile=MyCombinedProfile
   ```

Planetiler will output a single MBTiles file just like tippecanoe, but it can handle far larger extracts (whole continents) and lets you write more sophisticated attribute logic (e.g., compute `class` values, join with external tables, etc.).

*Both pipelines produce the same kind of artifact:* an **MBTiles** (or **PMTiles**) archive that MapLibre can consume with a `type: "vector"` source.

---

## 4️⃣ Serve the single tileset

| Option | How to use it in MapLibre |
|--------|---------------------------|
| **tileserver-gl** (Node) | `url: "http://myserver/tiles/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf"` |
| **TileServer-PHP** | Same URL pattern, works with Apache/Nginx |
| **PMTiles** (static file) | `url: "https://mycdn.com/combined.pmtiles"` and add `type: "vector"` with `url: "pmtiles://combined.pmtiles"` (requires the `pmtiles` protocol plugin) |
| **Cloud-native (S3 + CloudFront)** | Host the MBTiles/PMTiles file as a static object; use the `pmtiles` protocol or a tiny Lambda edge to serve tile ranges |

Example source definition:

```json
{
  "id": "combined",
  "type": "vector",
  "url": "pmtiles://https://cdn.example.com/combined.pmtiles",
  "maxzoom": 14,
  "minzoom": 5
}
```

---

## 5️⃣ Style the combined source

Because you kept the original layer names (`roads`, `water`, `labels`, `delivery_zones`), you can style each independently in the same style JSON:

```json
{
  "version": 8,
  "sources": {
    "combined": {
      "type": "vector",
      "url": "pmtiles://https://cdn.example.com/combined.pmtiles"
    }
  },
  "layers": [
    { "id": "water-fill", "type": "fill", "source": "combined", "source-layer": "water", "paint": { "fill-color": "#a0c8f0" } },
    { "id": "road-line", "type": "line", "source": "combined", "source-layer": "roads", "paint": { "line-color": "#777", "line-width": 2 } },
    { "id": "label-place", "type": "symbol", "source": "combined", "source-layer": "labels", "layout": { "text-field": ["get", "name"] }, "paint": { "text-color": "#000" } },
    { "id": "delivery-zones", "type": "fill", "source": "combined", "source-layer": "delivery_zones", "paint": { "fill-color": "#ff6600", "fill-opacity": 0.3 } }
  ]
}
```

Insert your custom layer **before** the first symbol layer if you want your polygons to appear under the basemap labels (or after if you want them on top).

---

## 6️⃣ Drawbacks of a single-source tileset (why you usually don’t want it)

| Issue | Why it matters |
|-------|----------------|
| **Re-building cost** | Any change to your delivery zones forces a full rebuild of the whole tileset (including the basemap). With a two-source approach you only rebuild the small `delivery_zones` tileset. |
| **Basemap updates** | Hosted basemap providers (MapTiler, OpenFreeMap, etc.) regularly refresh roads, water, and labels. If you bake them into your own MBTiles you miss those updates unless you rebuild. |
| **Licensing & attribution** | By redistributing OSM data you inherit OSM’s attribution requirements for the entire combined file. Keeping the basemap separate lets you rely on the provider’s attribution handling. |
| **File size** | Even with aggressive simplification, a global or continental basemap + your polygons can be several hundred MB. A separate, tiny `delivery_zones.mbtiles` is usually < 10 MB. |
| **Cache friendliness** | Browsers and CDNs cache each source independently. If only your polygons change, the basemap tiles stay cached. A monolithic file forces a full re-download. |

Only consider the single-source pipeline when **offline/air-gapped** operation, **demo-only** deployments, or **very small geographic extents** (e.g., a single city where the basemap is a few MB) make the extra build effort worthwhile.

---

## 📚 TL;DR Checklist

1. **Decide if you really need one source.**  
   *Most apps: keep basemap + your data separate.*

2. **If you need a single tileset:**  
   - Extract & filter OSM data (osmconvert/osmium).  
   - Prepare/simplify your delivery-zone polygons (GeoJSON → simplified).  
   - Generate two MBTiles with **Tippecanoe** (or one with **Planetiler**).  
   - Merge them with **tile-join** (or let Planetiler output the merged file).  
   - Host the resulting MBTiles/PMTiles via a tile server or static CDN.  
   - Reference it as a `vector` source in your MapLibre style and style each layer by its original name.

3. **Remember the trade-offs:** rebuild cost, stale basemap data, licensing, and file size.

---

### Further reading & tools

| Category | Tool / Link |
|----------|-------------|
| OSM extraction & filtering | `osmconvert`, `osmium`, `osmfilter` |
| GeoJSON simplification | `mapshaper`, `ogr2ogr -simplify`, `turf.simplify` |
| Vector-tile generation | **Tippecanoe** – <https://github.com/felt/tippecanoe> |
| Tile merging | **tile-join** (bundled with tippecanoe) |
| High-performance pipeline | **Planetiler** – <https://github.com/onthegomap/planetiler> |

If you decide later that the two-source pattern is sufficient (the usual case), just drop the merge step and point your style at the hosted basemap URL plus a separate `geojson` or `vector` source for the delivery zones. That gives you instant updates, smaller builds, and far less operational overhead.
